explanation: Fires mainly in CSS property declarations, on the colon or the space right after a dimension property name (height, width, left, top, min-width), just before a small numeric value such as 0 or 1px. Weaker on other code key/value separators (=, ":", rotate(, 2>&1) and on spaces before numbers in prose. Ordinary prose tokens give little or nothing.

Fires on the first token of a new sentence or clause, especially right after a paragraph break, opening quote or dash: opening quote+word (“For, "That, “But), 'that' in 'At that time'/'During that meeting', and '—for', '–and'. Also fires on odd symbols such as ™ and arrows. Mid-sentence content tokens are weak.

Fires on a word-completing subword piece whose identity is almost fixed by the preceding piece(s): 'nil' after 'err !=', 'ly' in Firstly/initially, '\le' in \leq, the middle of chemical or rare names (naphth, xanth, Nha Tr-ang), 'Woman' after 'Wonder'. Strength tracks how predictable the continuation is, not its meaning.

Fires on word-final suffix pieces that complete a word, such as -ves (scarves, curves, cleaves), -ator (activator) and -vents. It also fires moderately on 'filed' in legal contexts (a lawsuit filed, was filed). Other tokens are weak.

Strongest on the '[' that opens an Objective-C message send after '=' or 'return' ([NSOperationQueue new], [super init]). It also fires fairly strongly on a scattered mix of tokens: titles like 'Chairman', 'out of', word-ending subwords, '= types.bool', '&' in Go 'return &'. There is no clear common thread beyond the ObjC bracket.

Fires on many unrelated tokens with no clear shared property: Russian and Turkish word-internal pieces (ути-лит-ой, окруж-ност-ям), 'e.g', the start of a question after 'Q:', 'have been', 'per year', 'I agree' and similar. I can't predict its activity well.

Fires on distinctive named-entity or topical noun tokens, often the first piece of a less common word: 'undercover', 'bipartisan', 'boycotted', 'wholesalers', 'Bollywood', 'Taliban', 'Billboard', 'sitcom', 'syslog', 'heterozygous'. The main trigger is a specific, semantically loaded noun or modifier, and 'undercover' is the clearest case.

Fires on the separator just before an identifier, code or number in an ID-like or alphanumeric label: the space in 'ID 1' and 'No. 3', the '-' in HLA-A or Na,K-ATPase, '_' in snake_case names, the 'A' in 'No. A047'. Weaker on 'and' or spaces before numbers in lists and dates.

Fires on word-internal subword pieces of biochemical and biomedical technical terms: ty-ros-ine, flag-ell-um/in, perox-is-ome, car-box-ylase, glucopyran-os-ide, Angelica-e, spl-en-ectomized. Weaker on other jargon fragments (PKCS, USSD) and plain words.

Fires on a mixture of tokens: citation-key pieces such as '@pgen', '@ppat', '@CR' and 'U.S. Pat. No', 'Scanner' after 'new', 'opensource' in license URLs, 'Caco-2', and some function words in prose. There is no clear common feature.

Fires in the opening of biographical encyclopedia entries: the en dash between birth and death dates ('(17 June 1921 – 28 May'), the last digit of a birth or death year, 'people' in 'Notable people with the surname', 'born', and 'births' in category lines. Moderate on birth-year digits in 'born ... 19xx' outside the lead.

Fires on a word-initial subword fragment that starts a longer word: mostly 're' in technical words (reductase, resection, reactivation, reed). It also fires on the first piece of foreign or rare proper names (Ja-afar, B-ongaigaon, Kh-uzestan, Wh-etoi, CO-UCH). Whole common words are weak.

Fires on content words in socioeconomic and policy discussion, such as 'handicapped', 'crisis', 'high-income earners', 'overseas', 'hungry', 'deprivation'. It also fires on Objective-C/.NET identifiers such as 'ManagedObjectContext', ')viewDidLoad' and 'AssemblyProduct'. These are two unrelated triggers.

Fires on the second subword piece of a proper name or foreign word, especially 'ar' in names like Oskar and Asghar, and pieces such as af-ghan, O-con, Ogh-am, Alban-ian, A-Arch, Arab-id-opsis. Weak on whole common words.

Fires in Q&A and technical-forum prose right after a code block or at a clause boundary: the token that restarts explanatory prose ('Note', 'Here', 'These', 'In', 'I', 'you', 'This approach') and commas after an intro phrase ('In this query,', 'Using this technique,'). Weak inside code and in narrative text.

Fires on digits inside long identifier numbers in citations: the middle digits of US patent numbers ('U.S. Pat. No. 5,42[4],054'), patent URLs, PLoS article IDs, and the space or digits in legal reporter citations ('774 F.2d 456'). Weak on algebra variables and plain prose.

Fires on many different tokens: 'ant' prefixes completing words (antiques, antiepileptic, entice), 'Town' in Cape Town, 'y' in Forty/Seventy, 'to' after 'confused as' or 'want'. There is no clear common feature.

Fires on separators and closing pieces at the end of a list item or parenthetical, especially commas and close-parens after a list element or formula ('Gomes,', '(Fe3+),', '\},', '(4F2):') and quotes or commas in quoted lists. It also fires on scattered tokens such as 'companies' in 'the two companies'. Mostly list or enumeration punctuation, with noise.

Fires on a wide range of tokens in formal expository text (political affiliations like 'Labour', 'liberal', 'Biden', 'administration'; medical terms like 'implantation', 'intrauterine'; prepositions like 'of', 'from', 'after'). They don't share any clear property.

Fires on the verb of the idioms 'take place' and 'take effect' ('took' or 'taken' right before 'place' or 'effect'), and on 'into' in 'came into effect' and 'take into account/consideration'. Weak elsewhere.

Fires on a capital or lowercase first letter split off as its own token at the start of a word, especially K, S, E, k and s (K|uala, K|enny, S|uspended, k|ailasa, s|ipped), often after a space, slash or line break. It is weaker on other split initials.
